title: Section 120 — Voluntarily causing hurt or grievous hurt to extort confession, or to compel restoration of property

content.overview: BNS s. 120 — Voluntarily causing hurt or grievous hurt to extort confession, or to compel restoration of property.
content.study:
Introduction and meaning
Voluntarily causing hurt or grievous hurt to extort a confession or information, or to compel restoration of property. Historical concordance: IPC sections 330 and 331. For conduct governed by the BNS, cite section 120; use the IPC provisions only as historical concordance.
In student language: BNS s. 120 is the rule on “Voluntarily causing hurt or grievous hurt to extort confession, or to compel restoration of property”. The section provides that (1) Whoever voluntarily causes hurt for the purpose of extorting from the sufferer or from any person interested in the sufferer, any confession or any information which may lead to the detection of an offence or misconduct, or for the purpose of constraining the sufferer or any person interested in the sufferer to restore or to cause the restoration of any property or valuable security or to satisfy any claim or demand, or to give information which may lead to the restoration of any property or valuable security, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to seven years, and shall also be liable to fine. Do not stop at the heading. An examiner awards marks for the ingredients, the explanations and the illustrations, not for writing the title alone.

Why this is asked
Criminal law arguments turn on statutory ingredients. BNS s. 120 exists so that “Voluntarily causing hurt or grievous hurt to extort confession, or to compel restoration of property” has a closed legal test in Chapter VI — Of Offences Affecting the Human Body. An authoritative analysis defines the concept, lists every ingredient, walks the statutory illustrations, states exceptions, and applies the test methodically to facts.
Chapter setting: Homicide, organised crime, terrorism, hurt, acid, restraint, assault, kidnapping and trafficking.

The provision in detail
120. (1) Whoever voluntarily causes hurt for the purpose of extorting from the sufferer or from any person interested in the sufferer, any confession or any information which may lead to the detection of an offence or misconduct, or for the purpose of constraining the sufferer or any person interested in the sufferer to restore or to cause the restoration of any property or valuable security or to satisfy any claim or demand, or to give information which may lead to the restoration of any property or valuable security, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to seven years, and shall also be liable to fine

(2) Whoever voluntarily causes grievous hurt for any purpose referred to in sub-section (1), shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to ten years, and shall also be liable to fine

Essential ingredients
1. (1) Whoever voluntarily causes hurt for the purpose of extorting from the sufferer or from any person interested in the sufferer, any confession or any information which may lead to the detection of an offence or misconduct, or for the purpose of constraining the sufferer or any person interested in the sufferer to restore or to cause the restoration of any property or valuable security or to satisfy any claim or demand, or to give information which may lead to the restoration of any property or valuable security, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to seven years, and shall also be liable to fine
2. (2) Whoever voluntarily causes grievous hurt for any purpose referred to in sub-section (1), shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to ten years, and shall also be liable to fine

Statutory illustrations
Illustration (a). A, a police officer, tortures Z in order to induce Z to confess that he committed a crime. A is guilty of an offence under this section

Exam use: quote illustration (a), then write which ingredient of BNS s. 120 it proves. Copying the illustration without that mapping sentence does not score.

Illustration (c). A, a revenue officer, tortures Z in order to compel him to pay certain arrears of revenue due from Z. A is guilty of an offence under this section

learningObjectives: Master the statutory shield against custodial torture and forced confessions under BNS s. 120.
Analyze the twin purposes: extorting a confession/information, or compelling restoration of property/valuable security.
Distinguish sub-section (1) (hurt: up to 7 years and fine) from sub-section (2) (grievous hurt: up to 10 years and fine).
Connect Section 120 with Article 20(3) of the Constitution (privilege against self-incrimination).
enhancement.definition: BNS s. 120 consolidates offences protecting against custodial torture and coerced confessions: sub-section (1) punishes voluntarily causing hurt for the purpose of extorting any confession or information which may lead to the detection of an offence or misconduct, or constraining the restoration of property or valuable security, with imprisonment up to seven years and fine; sub-section (2) punishes voluntarily causing grievous hurt for any such purpose with imprisonment up to ten years and fine.
enhancement.legalPrinciple: Prohibits third-degree methods, custodial violence, and private torture by criminalizing physical harm inflicted to extract confessions, information, or property restoration.
statutoryFramework: Chapter VI — Of Offences Affecting the Human Body, BNS s. 120 (consolidating IPC ss. 330 and 331).
Sub-section (1): Voluntarily causing hurt to extort confession or compel restoration — imprisonment of either description up to seven years, and fine.
Sub-section (2): Voluntarily causing grievous hurt to extort confession or compel restoration — imprisonment of either description up to ten years, and fine.
Constitutional nexus: Protects the fundamental right against self-incrimination under Article 20(3) and the right to life/dignity under Article 21.
Statutory illustration: A police officer tortures a suspect to induce a confession of a crime; the officer is guilty under this section.
essentialIngredients: The accused voluntarily caused hurt (sub-section 1) OR grievous hurt (sub-section 2).
The act was done for the purpose of extorting any confession or information which may lead to the detection of an offence or misconduct; OR
For the purpose of constraining the sufferer or an interested person to restore or cause restoration of any property or valuable security, or satisfy any claim.
enhancement.detailedExplanation: Section 120 consolidates former IPC 330 and 331. It is a vital statutory weapon against third-degree methods and custodial torture. While commonly invoked against police officers or investigating authorities who torture suspects or witnesses to extract confessions or reveal stolen property, the section is not limited to public servants—it applies equally to private individuals (e.g., village panchayat members or private citizens torturing someone suspected of theft). The purpose is strictly defined: extorting a confession or information regarding an offence or misconduct, or compelling the return of property or satisfaction of a claim. Sub-section (1) punishes simple hurt with up to seven years imprisonment; sub-section (2) punishes grievous hurt with up to ten years imprisonment and fine.
examples: Teaching example (Custodial third-degree): An investigating police officer beats a theft suspect with leather straps and suspends him from a ceiling hook in police custody to force him to sign a confession. The officer is guilty under s. 120(1).

Teaching example (Private vigilante torture causing fracture): Village residents catch a youth suspected of stealing a motorcycle, tie him to a pole, and beat him with sticks until his arm fractures, demanding that he disclose where the motorcycle is parked. The residents are guilty under s. 120(2) (grievous hurt to compel restoration of property).
distinctions: Section 120 vs Section 119: Section 119 covers extorting property unlawfully; Section 120 covers extracting confessions, information leading to detection of crime, or compelling restoration of property legitimately claimed.
Section 120 vs Section 121: Section 121 protects public servants from being deterred; Section 120 protects citizens from public servants (or others) using torture to extract confessions.
problemApplication: Issue: Whether a revenue inspector who subjected a clerk to physical beatings causing broken ribs to force him to confess to embezzling municipal funds is liable under s. 120.
Rule: Causing grievous hurt to extort a confession or information regarding misconduct constitutes an offence under BNS s. 120(2).
Application: Rib fractures constitute grievous hurt under s. 116(g), and the beating was inflicted specifically to extract a confession of misconduct.
Conclusion: The revenue inspector is guilty under BNS s. 120(2) and liable to up to ten years imprisonment.
